_comment: Ordered gap-repair queue, consumed by backfill_gp_history.py once the
forward frontier has caught up to the rolling end (today - 7d).
Ordered by VALUE DENSITY, not chronology. The frontier keeps the live
boundary closed by itself; this queue exists for the holes behind it.
Every segment below was measured, not assumed — bounded epoch-range
counts over the 194M-row archive on 2026-08-08. Density is stated as
DISTINCT SATELLITES per day, not rows: a 2026-08 day has 3x the rows of
a 2026-05 day while covering FEWER satellites, because Starlink SupGP
publishes 5-8 versions per object at a shared epoch. Row count is the
misleading axis and it is why this hole looked like a recovery.
which round-trips through the release asset like the frontier does. The
queue DEFINITION lives here in git so it is reviewable; only the
Re-running a covered day is safe and cheap on our side: the consumer
inserts under UNIQUE(satellite_id, epoch), so existing rows are skipped.
It is NOT free upstream, which is why the segments are bounded to what

segments.label: G3-2026-01-outage
segments.why: Total live-path outage: 2026-01-21..27 holds 15-452 rows/day (and the same number of distinct satellites), then 5-17k rows / 5-10k sats/day through 02-23. Unreachable until now: BACKFILL_START was hard-coded to 2026-02-27, so neither the frontier nor a repair run could ever touch it.

segments.label: probe-2012-11
segments.why: PROBE, not repair. Monthly counts step from 438-480k (2012-01..10) to 270k (2012-11) and stay at 210-273k through 2013. Three days first: if the upstream returns the same thin counts we already hold, the step is real history (fewer objects tracked, or an 18 SPCS publication change) and the 426-day segment below should be dropped rather than run.

segments.label: 2012-11-to-2013-step
segments.why: The sustained ~46% density step the probe above tests. Gated on that probe: drop this segment if the probe shows upstream has no more than we do.

segments.label: scattered-2020-11
segments.why: Rolling-median outlier; recent enough that the objects are still on orbit and the data is still useful for constellation work.

segments.label: scattered-1986-summer
segments.why: Rolling-median outlier. Lowest value of the set — pre-LEO-constellation era — deliberately ordered last before the multi-year block.

segments.label: G5-2001-to-2004
segments.why: The largest remaining job and the lowest density-per-request: 39 months at ~72k/month against a ~290k/month baseline, i.e. 75% missing, ~8.5M rows. Ordered last on purpose — everything above closes a hole that current LEO research can actually use, this one closes a hole in the pre-constellation record.
